proposals.subject: Bathynomus giganteus
proposals.title: It has moved again
proposals.body: I went round the whip coral. It swung into my path. I went round it again. We are both still exactly where it lives.

media.sourceCaption:
A giant deep-sea isopod, Bathynomus giganteus, with an antipatharian whip coral, Stichopathes sp., in the foreground, seen during the Gulf of Mexico 2017 expedition. While the isopod imaged here was spotted during exploration of a site dubbed “Okeanos Ridge,” the team saw several of these throughout the expedition and even managed to catch footage of one swimming.
From: Gulf of Mexico 2017: Highlight Images.

proposals.alt: A pale giant isopod stands on sediment behind a curling orange whip coral that crosses the foreground.
proposals.canon: Boris remains Bathynomus giganteus in the deep Gulf of Mexico. Source identifies B. giganteus and Stichopathes sp. at Okeanos Ridge during Gulf of Mexico2017. No new sex, life stage, mate or home is established.
proposals.chronology: Append after his existing gentle-arrival video and smaller-fish-head gift post. Preserve both literal bodies and avatar.
proposals.fictionBoundary: The still documents the isopod, coral and foreground overlap. Walking around the coral, its swing, the second detour and irritation are fiction. No documented contact, measured current or photographed movement sequence is claimed. The coral remains attached, not a crawling animal.
proposals.biologyBasis: Black corals have flexible skeletons and attach to hard substrate. This supports limited current-driven bending, not a claim that this exact coral swung as described. Do not substitute octocoral anatomy or assert a measured bend amplitude.
proposals.distinctness: Boris’s existing episodes concern an overbearing arrival and an edible gift. Here a small spatial detour becomes a repeated negotiation with an attached neighbor. No rescue, protection or meal frustration.

sourceReviews.sourceCaption:
Towards the end of Dive 11 of the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition, we moved from stable ripples and pavement to softer sediments with smaller fractions of broken paleo reef. The seafloor here was pockmarked with circular patches of turned-over sediments, and we also observed larger scar marks that were likely feeding holds for fish and/or Chaceon crabs — like the one pictured here.
Learn more
